Need for Immediate Central Assistance to Tackle Unprecedented drought in 
Karnataka 
SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN (Karnataka): Mr. Chairman, Sir, Karnataka 
is facing unprecedented drought for the third consecutive year. During the entire 
period from January to December 2003, out of 176 Taluks, 161 Taluks in Karnataka 
have received less rains, causing deficiency of about 23 per cent rainfall in the 
State. In Septebmer and November 2003, the rainfall has been the lowest of the 
last 30 years. Due to dry spells, 42 pe r cent of the standing kharif crops and 
36.5 per cent of rabi crops have been affected. The total damage assessed for 
horticulture crop is Rs. 3974.39 crores. A delegation comprising members of 
the Cabinet Sub-Committee on Management of drought in Karnataka and 
Members of Parliament both from Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha met the hon. 
Prime Minister, the Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission and the Minister for 
Agriculture on 17th and 18th December, 2003 to personally apprise them about 
the seriousness of the prevailing situation of drought in Karnataka for the third 
successive year. Even after the strong plea made by the State Government, 
the Central Government has released only Rs. 115.86 crores as against the 
request of Rs. 1881.55 crores. On 29.12.2003, another 1.65 lakh metric tonnes of 
rice were released as against the request of 9.9 lakh metric tonnes. It is an injustice 
done to the poor farmers in the State of Karnataka. Therefore, I urge upon the 
Central Government to take immediate measures to provide requested financial 
assistance and release foodgrains immediately. I would request you to kindly 
see to it that the Government acts immediately.

preparing for various competitive examinations of the SSC, UPSC, Banking 
Service Commision, State PSCs, etc., and they were getting jobs. But, now, 
competitive examinations are hardly held. On the contrary, the VRS has become 
the order of the day, and abolition of posts has become a routine in Government

Threat posed due to import of toxic Industrial waste 
SHRI B. J. PANDA (Orissa): Sir, India is increasinglybecoming a preferred 
dumping ground for toxic industrial waste from developed countries, which poses a 
serious threat to our public health and environment. While developed countries 
have banned its use because of its devastating impact on their public health, we seem 
to think that we need every dollar and every job that is created out of it. The brain-
damaging mercury, toxic electronics, plastic wastes, cancer-causing asbestos, 
defective steel and tin plates, toxic waste oil, used batteries and scrap of metals 
from developed countries dumped on us have increased manifold. According to 
studies, every year, 1,00,000 tonnes of hazardous wastes enter India in gross 
violation of the 1997 Supreme Court order banning such import. Mercury causes 
severe and permanent damage to the central nervous system, lungs and kidneys, 
triggers depression and suicidal tendencies and causes paralysis. It has severely 
contaminated land, water, air and t he food chain throughout the country. Raw 
asbestos, banned in all developed countries, is imported to the extent of around 
one lakh tonnes per annum. It causes fatal diseases including lung cancer and 
many other ailments. Even in our Factories Act, 1948, asbestos has been listed 
as a disease-causing substance. More appalling is that while our country is now the 
major dumping ground of these hazardous wastes, Government has not thought it 
fit to regulate its trade and use. It is high time that India took a serious look into 
this problem to address this issue in our overall national interest.

SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION 
Unemployment problem in the country 
SHRI JIBON ROY (West Bengal): Thank You, Mr. Chairman, Sir, for 
giving me an opportunity to participate in the short duration discussion on the 
unemployment problem in the country. 
May be, this is going to be my last speech to the Members of the 
Treasury Benches who are sitting on my left in their capacity. After some time, 
they may be sitting on my right. Therefore, I seek some compassion from you 
while speaking. The second thing,, Sir, is that I do  not know as to why the 
Labour Minister has come to hear and reply to such a critical issue which has 
become the most menacing issue to this nation, to this country. Now, job riots are 
taking place, and it is taking the form of linguistic riots in some of the places. And, 
policy questions are involved in it. What will be the direction of the ec onomy, 
whether the Government will make public investment or not, what will be its 
technology policy, etc.? I do not think the Labour Minister is in a position to reply 
to all those questions, and, hence, I would request that either the Prime Minister 
or the Finance Minister should reply to this debate because, this debate does not 
pertain to the Labour Ministry alone. I do not wish to make politics out of the 
unemployment problem that is prevailing in the country. But, Sir, the 
Government is playing with the poorest of the poor of this country by declaring 
everyday that every year they are giving employment to one crore people. That 
is simply rubbing salt to the injury of the poor and the unemployed youth. They 
should stop doing it. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI RAMA SHANKER KAUSHIK) in the 
Chair.] 
What is happening? My esteemed friends who are sitting on my right 
are hot the angels, but the fact is that  during the period between 1992-97, the 
number of registered unemployed people did not move for five years. It was 3.9 
crores in the year 1998, and around 2 lakh people 
31 

RAJYA SABHA            [3 February, 2004] 
were getting employment during that period. But, in 2000, the figure jumped up to 
4.16 crores and the rate of employment was only 99,000. Sic, the rate of growth 
of employment is declining, and the unemployment rate is increasing every year. 
Between 1983-94, the growth rate of unemployment was around 0.8 per cent; 
sometimes it was minus, it has gone down, that means, at least, a good number 
of people who were coming to the employment market were getting 
employment. But is it happening today? The growth rate has gone down from 2.7 
per cent of 1.07 per cent in 1998. And now, the Ahluwalia Committee have said 
that the growth rate is 'nil' so far as employment is concerned. Such a serious and 
dangerous situation had developed in the country and our Prime Minister is going 
on making statements everyday that one crore people are getting employment 
every year. Sir, I have seen many Prime Ministers. But I have not seen one who 
has acquired such a terrific virtue of lying to the people; I have not seen or heard 
any Prime Minister before that! The Planning Commission is saying one thing, the 
Finance Ministry Report is saying one thing, but he is un dauntingly going on 
saying 'one crore, one crore, one crore1 and thus, he is hurting the poor people 
and unemployed youth. 
Sir, Articles 41, 42 and 43 of our Constitution have said that the Directive 
Principles of State Policy will be to grant the right to work as a fundamental 
right. Though it was not given as a fundamental right, the Directive Principles of 
State Policy is to give right to work, right to education, as fundamental rights and to 
act towards that. That was the 'Directive Principles of State Policy' according to 
the Constitution. I wish to know from t he Government whether they still hold that 
opinion or they are going to change the Constitution itself. The thing is employment 
in the organized sector is going down at an average of one lakh every year. During 
the last four years, employment has gone down by four lakhs in the organized 
sector. Your report says so, and now, there is no increase or improvement in the 
employment situation. 
Then employment is going down at the Central Government, State 
Governments even the local self-Governments, and the public sector. But from 
where have those one crore people who got employment come? Are those people 
in the heavens or in the sky or on the ear th—Prime Minister should explain that 
position; your Government should explain that position. 
The other day, Mr. Singhania, President of the Small Scale Industries had 
said that during the last four to five years, around three crores of

people? Would you please, explain? Employment in agriculture has gone down. 
Now negative growth is taking place. Therefore, it is time that the Government 
considered whether there was need to make any policy shift over the matter, on 
that binding issue. Why was I telling that Government should think over whether 
the policy they are pursuing was correct? It is a matter of policy. There had been

During the period 1983—94, in those t en years, there was growth in

SHRI N. JOTHI (Tamil Nadu): Madam, I am not going to speak much on this 
issue as all of us are aware of this problem. We all know that, next to the problem 
of population, the problem of unemployment is the biggest problem which is being 
faced by our country. But, what is the solution for that? That is the only thing we 
have to focus on. How should we focus on this problem? What are the remedial 
measures we have thought about it? On my part, I would like to contribute a little 
on this issue. We know that unemployment is of various kinds, like educated 
unemployment, urban unemployment, etc. So, these are various categories of 
unemployment. There is another type of unemployment, women unemployment; 
this issue is very vital. There are various kinds of unemployment. We can analyse 
this sector-wise. But how to give them employment? 
Now we are in the age of automation. Everything is on the feather-touch. 
We have brought in Coca Cola. We have brought in Pepsi. Pesticides are always 
there in it. It has killed hundreds of local aerated water works. Like that, without 
any vision, without any thinking, we have allowed them. I am not saying that the 
people who have brought it are bad people. I only say that they could have thought 
twice. It has led to this situation; and the local employment has been lost on that 
count. 
Madam, I can suggest one solution. We can think of giving tariff relief on 
man-made things. We can give duty relief on those items, for example, match 
industry in Sivakasi area in Tamil Nadu, which is very predominant. Two 
districts are in match industry-Thirunaveli and Kahyakumari. On the manmade 
matches, the duty is less. On the machine-made matches, the duty is more. Like that, 
we can bring in certain remedial meas ures. Wherever human employment is 
involved, we can always give some tax relief to them so that the policy to give more 
and more employment opportunities is adopted. We can think on these lines. 
Even today, handmade matches cost less. In the market also, the price is less 
on the handmade matchboxes than on the automation made matchboxes. Like 
that, we can think on these matters. 
Madam, when we think about unemployment, there is nothing wrong in 
feeling myself proud about my leader in our State, regarding women 
employment. Twenty-five women joined together and formed a group for self-
employment. The Government gives a substantial aid to them. The Government 
also guarantees bank loan for that group and many women

SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA (West Bengal): Madam, Mr. Singhal is 
right in saying that, perhaps, it has become a ritual to discuss about 
unemployment. It has become a ritual because, however seriously we may 
express our anxiety, whatever seriousness we may add to this problem, we 
cannot act, we cannot decide about the policies. It is the Government which 
has to take a lesson from this situation.  The Government has to resort to some 
policies so that a formidable solution could be arrived at in resolving this 
perennial problem of unemployment. 
(THE VICE-CHAIRMAN, DR. A.K. PATEL, in the Chair) 
Unfortunately, it has not happened. No proper action could be resorted to 
by this Government in the last four or five years. Even before the elections, the 
Government has pledged to the nation that it will generate at least one crore jobs 
every year. Now, we shall have to look at the balance-sheet. When the 
Government has decided to dissolve the Lok Sabha, when they are trying to 
absolve them from the responsibility of answering to the Parliament, we must 
look at the balance-sheet as to what exactly has happened. In fact, the situation, 
as on today, in so far as the unemployment problem is concerned, is deplorably 
poor. The hon. Labour Minister is sitting over here. He may, perhaps, agree with 
me that the unemployment situation or the employment situation is deplorably 
poor in the country of ours. It is very unfortunate that millions and millions of young 
men and women have been rendered unemployed or they are roaming around 
unemployed. There are no jobs at all. Even the Leader of the Opposition is saying 
that. Even the Planning Commission in its recent observation has stated that there 
are 21 crores of young men and women, in the country, between the age of 16 
years and 26 years, and during the intervening period of five or six years, hardly 
23.6 per cent of them could be employed, and that too, in the unorganised sector 
or in the informal sector. Only 9.6 per cent could be employed in the formal sector 
or in the organised sector where at least a minimum guarantee of jobs is there. 
Even then, the security of job is something which is completely missing during the 
regime of this NDA Government in the last three years. Sir, You will certainly 
appreciate that this unemployment problem is inextricably linked with the 
economic policy that this Government pursues. In fact, the Labour Minister has 
nothing to do with it. Here, in the morning, some of my revered colleagues raised 
this point that, in fact, the Labour Minister

concerned with the problems of labour; he was concerned with the problems of 
workers. There also he has totally failed. Not only that he has failed but also the
